name: Feynman's cargo cult science
scope: The 1974 Caltech commencement address that gave self-deception a name and an image. T1: Feynman describes South Sea islanders who, after the war, built the FORM of an airfield -- runways with fires along the sides, a wooden hut, a man sitting in it with two wooden pieces on his head like headphones and bars of bamboo sticking out like antennas -- and waited for the cargo planes; 'the form is perfect... But it doesn't work. No airplanes land.' T2: the sentence the whole strand hangs on -- 'The first principle is that you must not fool yourself -- and you are the easiest person to fool' -- with its second half: after you've not fooled yourself, it's easy not to fool other scientists. T3: the Millikan creep -- Millikan's measured charge on the electron was slightly too low because he used a wrong value for the viscosity of air, and the published measurements after him crept UP toward the truth in small steps instead of jumping; Feynman's diagnosis is the mechanism rung: 'When they got a number that was too high above Millikan's, they thought something must be wrong -- and they would look for and find a reason why something might be wrong. When they got a number closer to Millikan's value they didn't look so hard.' T4: the rat-maze rung -- Young's corridor experiment, where rats kept finding the right door until Young hunted down the hidden cue: 'He finally found that they could tell by the way the floor sounded when they ran over it. And he could only fix that by putting his corridor in sand.' T5: Feynman's point about that experiment -- almost nobody repeated or cited it; the field kept running rat studies WITHOUT the controls Young had proved were necessary, which is exactly the bamboo-antenna failure in a lab coat. T6: 'leaning over backwards' -- 'a kind of scientific integrity, a principle of scientific thought that corresponds to a kind of utter honesty', meaning you report everything that might make your result wrong, every alternative you ruled out, every thing that didn't work. T7: the honest-advertising contrast -- Feynman's Wesson oil example, an ad that is literally true and still misleads (the oil doesn't soak through food at a certain temperature -- but no oil does at that temperature); technically-true is not honest. T8: the address became the closing chapter of 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!' (1985), which is why the phrase escaped into ordinary English. T9: what 'cargo cult' diagnoses in practice -- rituals of science (graphs, jargon, a control group named but not used, p-values) performed without the one control that could have shown you were wrong. T10: the address's ending -- Feynman wishes the graduates 'the good luck to be somewhere where you are free' to keep that integrity, an admission that institutions can make honesty expensive. T11: myth guard -- 'cargo cult' movements (John Frum on Tanna, Vanuatu) were real Melanesian religious movements, not a joke Feynman invented, but his telling is a stylized parable, not fieldwork. T12: the personal version a kid can run -- before you announce a result, write down what you would have had to see to conclude the opposite.
source: Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science', Caltech 1974 commencement address, full text at calteches.library.caltech.edu/51/2/CargoCult.htm (verbatim quotes pulled from this primary text); Wikipedia 'Cargo cult science'. Grokipedia (grokipedia.com) returned HTTP 403 to the harness on every page attempted this session -- corroborate on Grokipedia during the build research stage before authoring.
framing_note: THE flagship voice ladder for the whole sub-strand. Voice: T1 keys the IMAGE (wooden headphones, bamboo antennas) -- the answer is the name Feynman gave that failure, never a definition of pseudoscience. Accuracy rail: every Feynman line must be quoted EXACTLY from the Caltech text or paraphrased plainly -- no invented Feynman aphorisms, and do not attribute 'cargo cult science' to a book he wrote in 1974 (it was a spoken address, printed later). Second rail: Millikan's error was the viscosity-of-air constant, and the creep is a story about honest people, not fraud -- say it that way. Dinner-test payoff: T1 and T3 (the numbers crept because nobody looked hard when they agreed). Distractor mine: real adjacent labels and people -- Langmuir's 'pathological science', Popper's falsifiability, the Dunning-Kruger effect, publication bias, Occam's razor; and for T3, real rival explanations for the creeping numbers (better vacuum pumps, improved optics, fraud) so the answer 'they stopped hunting for errors when the number agreed' must be known, not deduced. Lane border: PHILOSOPHY owns demarcation-as-seminar-move (what makes a theory scientific); this ladder stays on Feynman's WORKING PRACTICE. Anti-restatement: the stem must never say 'form without substance' before asking what the islanders' runway illustrates.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank: the demarcation problem / pseudoscience as an epistemology topic. Guard by keying every rung to Feynman's concrete cases (the bamboo hut, the electron-charge creep, the sanded corridor), never to 'what makes a claim scientific'.

name: The Mesmer commission of 1784
scope: The first blinded experiment in history, run in Benjamin Franklin's garden. T1: a blindfolded boy is led around Franklin's garden at Passy and told to embrace four trees in turn to find the one a mesmerist has 'magnetized'; he swoons at the FOURTH tree -- the one nobody had touched (the hook: the fainting happened at the wrong tree). T2: what was being tested -- Franz Mesmer's claim that an invisible universal fluid, 'animal magnetism', flows between all bodies and dams up in the sick; his Paris salon ran on a baquet, an oak tub of magnetized water bristling with iron rods that patients gripped while music played, until they fell into convulsive 'crises' that were counted as the cure working. T3: in 1784 Louis XVI appointed a royal commission of the Academy of Sciences and the Faculty of Medicine, with Benjamin Franklin as its most famous member, the chemist Antoine Lavoisier, the astronomer Jean Sylvain Bailly (who drafted the report) and the physician Joseph-Ignace Guillotin. T4: Mesmer himself refused to be tested; his most prominent disciple, the court physician Charles d'Eslon, offered his own practice instead -- so the commission tested the doctrine on a believer's patients. T5: the cup-of-water test -- a woman given ordinary water while told it was magnetized had a full crisis; given genuinely magnetized water while told it was plain, she felt nothing. T6: the design insight that makes this the ancestor of every honest trial -- the commissioners realized the only way to separate the CLAIMED CAUSE from the patient's BELIEF was to control what the patient knew, so they cut the patient's knowledge away with a blindfold. T7: the verdict -- no evidence of any fluid whatsoever; the effects were real but produced by 'imagination', which is generally credited as the first scientific description of what we now call the placebo effect. T8: d'Eslon's startlingly modern reply -- he accepted the finding and argued that if imagination heals, imagination is worth studying. T9: the secret report -- a second, confidential report to the king warned of the moral danger of women held in convulsive crisis by male magnetizers, so the commission wrote the part it would not print. T10: the afterlife -- the debunked fluid left behind a real phenomenon: the mesmerists' trance was renamed and studied as hypnotism by James Braid in the 1840s, and Mesmer's name survives in the ordinary verb 'mesmerize'. T11: the Franklin twist worth its own rung -- the glass armonica whose eerie tone Mesmer used to bring on crises was an instrument Franklin himself had invented (verify at build before authoring).
source: Wikipedia 'Franz Mesmer' (1784 royal commissions, Franklin/Lavoisier/Bailly/Guillotin membership, d'Eslon as the tested party, blind trials, the imagination verdict as first observation of the placebo effect, the secret report); Wikipedia 'Animal magnetism', 'Benjamin Franklin', 'James Braid (surgeon)'. framing_note: Voice: T1 keys the ACT and its result (blindfolded boy, wrong tree) -- never a date and never 'who investigated Mesmer?'. Accuracy rail: Franklin was old and ill (gout and a stone) and hosted rather than personally performed every trial; Bailly wrote the report -- do not turn this into 'Franklin single-handedly debunks Mesmer'. Second rail: 'animal' in animal magnetism means anima/living, not beasts -- teach that before testing anything that turns on it. Third rail: the commission found the FLUID unproven, not that the patients were faking; their effects were genuine. Dinner-test payoff: T1, with T5 (the two cups of water) as the second. Distractor mine: live 18th-century rival forces a serious person could have named -- electricity, Newtonian gravitation and the tides, 'nervous fluid', phlogiston, the four humours, and actual iron magnets (Maximilian Hell's magnet cures, which Mesmer began from). Lane border: HISTORY owns the French Revolution and Franklin the diplomat; the fact that Lavoisier and Bailly were both guillotined in the Terror is TRUE but belongs to history -- use it at most as a one-line closing aside, never as a rung's answer.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank: Benjamin Franklin in France as American envoy; Lavoisier and Bailly executed in the Terror; the guillotine and Guillotin. Guard by keying every rung to the TEST DESIGN (blindfold, unlabeled cups, the untouched tree) rather than to any revolutionary-era event.

name: Clever Hans, the horse that read faces
scope: Psychology learned the double-blind from a horse. T1: Berlin, 1904 -- crowds watch a horse answer arithmetic by tapping his hoof, and a 13-member commission led by the psychologist Carl Stumpf, including a veterinarian, a circus manager, a cavalry officer and the director of the Berlin zoo, concludes there is no trickery (the hook: the experts found no fraud, and they were right -- there wasn't any). T2: the owner -- Wilhelm von Osten, a retired gymnasium mathematics teacher, amateur horse trainer and phrenologist, who charged no admission and believed every bit of it. T3: the repertoire -- Hans appeared to add, subtract, multiply, divide, handle fractions, tell the time, track the calendar, tell musical tones apart, and spell German, all in hoof taps. T4: Oskar Pfungst's decisive numbers, 1907 -- Hans was right 89% of the time (50 of 56) when he could see a questioner who knew the answer, and 6% (2 of 35) when he could not see the questioner; his accuracy tracked what the HUMAN knew, not what the horse knew. T5: the mechanism -- as the taps neared the right number, the questioner's head, posture and facial tension shifted involuntarily and released; Hans stopped on the release. Von Osten was signalling without knowing it, which is why he passed every test for cheating. T6: Pfungst's own capture -- once he had identified the cue he could produce it deliberately, and found he emitted it involuntarily even while trying not to. T7: what it changed -- the 'Clever Hans effect' is the reason a modern animal-cognition or drug trial is run so that the human in the room does not know the right answer either; the horse is the origin story of the double blind. T8: the modern rerun -- facilitated communication, in which an assistant supported the hand of a nonspeaking person at a keyboard, collapsed under a message-passing test: when the client and the facilitator were shown DIFFERENT pictures, the typed answer matched the facilitator's picture (verify the specific 1993 studies at build before authoring numbers).
source: Wikipedia 'Clever Hans' (von Osten's background, the 1904 Stumpf commission of 13, Pfungst's 1907 conditions, the 89%/50-of-56 and 6%/2-of-35 figures, the posture-release cue, the double-blind legacy); Wikipedia 'Facilitated communication' (message-passing tests) -- verify before authoring T8. Grokipedia 403 to the harness this session; re-check at build.
framing_note: Voice: the wonder is that NOBODY was lying -- an honest man and an honest horse fooled a commission of experts. T1 must key that (the commission found no deception and was correct), not 'who owned Clever Hans?'. Accuracy rail: Pfungst did not catch a cheat; he changed what the QUESTIONER knew. State the two conditions precisely -- the collapse happens both when Hans cannot see the questioner AND when the questioner is ignorant of the answer -- and do not report Hans as 'always wrong' (6% is near chance for tap counts, not zero). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the horse's score tracked the human's knowledge). Distractor mine: real adjacent explanations serious people held -- genuine equine numeracy, secret whistles or wires, trained memorization of question-sounds, smell, telepathy (a live claim in 1904), and Hawthorne/observer effects. Lane border: ANIMAL bank owns horse senses, social cognition and domestication -- this ladder keys the CONTROL, not the animal; a rung may state that Hans's real skill (reading tiny human body cues) is impressive, but must not become an animal-behaviour rung.
history_overlap: ANIMAL bank: horse cognition, equine perception of human body language, animal training. Guard by making every answer a feature of the EXPERIMENT (questioner ignorance, blinders, the involuntary cue) rather than a fact about horses.

name: N-rays and the anatomy of pathological science
scope: How a whole branch of physics can be seen by a hundred people and not exist. T1: 1903, University of Nancy -- Prosper-Rene Blondlot, a respected physicist, announces a new radiation; the detector is a faint spark or phosphorescent thread in a darkened room, judged BRIGHTER or dimmer by eye, and about 120 scientists go on to publish some 300 papers on it. T2: what N-rays supposedly did -- they poured out of nearly every substance (though not from green wood or certain treated metals), were emitted by the human nervous system, and could be stored in a brick; every claimed detection was a human judgement at the edge of visibility. T3: the sting operation -- in 1904 the American physicist Robert W. Wood visits the lab; in the dark he quietly removes the essential aluminium prism from the spectroscope, and the demonstrator reads off exactly the same N-ray spectrum; Wood also swaps the N-ray-emitting steel file for a piece of wood, and the 'rays' keep coming. T4: Wood publishes the visit in Nature on 29 September 1904 and the field evaporates within about a year -- 300 papers erased by one man's hand in the dark. T5: the twist -- in December 1904 the French Academy of Sciences still awarded Blondlot the Prix Leconte and its 50,000 francs, rewording the citation to honour 'the totality of his work' rather than the discovery of N-rays. T6: MYTH CORRECTION rung -- Blondlot did not go mad and die of shame; he kept his chair at Nancy until retiring in 1910, died in 1930 aged 81, and was reportedly still convinced of N-rays in 1926. T7: why the eye was the weak link -- the effect sat at the threshold of detection, in the dark, judged by an observer who knew what he hoped to see and knew when the apparatus was 'on'; nobody was blinded, so expectation WAS the instrument. T8: Irving Langmuir gave the pattern a name in a colloquium at the Knolls Research Laboratory on 18 December 1953 -- 'the science of things that aren't so' -- and the transcript was finally published in Physics Today in October 1989. T9: Langmuir's symptom list, the practical part -- the effect stays at the limit of detectability; its size does not grow when you strengthen the supposed cause; enormous accuracy is claimed; every failed replication is met with a fresh ad hoc excuse; and the ratio of believers rises, then fades to nothing. T10: polywater -- reported by Nikolai Fedyakin in 1961 and pushed by Boris Derjaguin, water condensed in fine quartz tubes seemed to freeze at -40C and boil at 150C, and by 1969 there was public fear it might convert the world's water; in 1971 Denis Rousseau compared its infrared spectrum with his own SWEAT after a handball game and found them identical -- it was contaminated water. T11: cold fusion -- Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons announced fusion in a jar at a University of Utah press conference on 23 March 1989, before peer review; laboratories worldwide could not reproduce the excess heat, and the claim did not survive replication.
source: Wikipedia 'N ray' (1903 announcement, ~120 scientists / ~300 papers, Wood's 1904 prism removal and the swapped file, Nature 29 September 1904, Blondlot still convinced in 1926); Wikipedia 'Prosper-Rene Blondlot' (Prix Leconte 1904, 50,000 francs, citation worded for 'the totality of his work', retired 1910, died 1930 aged 81); Wikipedia 'Pathological science' (Langmuir, Knolls Research Laboratory 18 December 1953, Physics Today October 1989, symptom list, cited cases); Wikipedia 'Polywater' (Fedyakin 1961, Derjaguin, claimed properties, 1969 scare, Rousseau's 1971 sweat comparison, clean-glassware resolution by 1973). framing_note: Voice: this is the strand's REVERSAL backbone -- T3 is the scene (a visitor palming a prism in the dark) and the answer is what happened next, not 'who debunked N-rays?'. Accuracy rail: Wood removed a prism AND swapped a file -- keep the two acts distinct and do not invent a third; and the Prix Leconte citation wording is the whole point of T5, so quote it as reported ('the totality of his work'). Third rail: the myth-correction rung is mandatory -- the widely repeated claim that Blondlot went insane and died in disgrace is false and must be told AS a myth. Fourth rail: on cold fusion say 'could not be reproduced' and 'mainstream physics rejects it', never 'fraud'. Dinner-test payoff: T3, with T10 (the sweat spectrum) as the second. Distractor mine: the real rays of that decade, all discovered within a few years of each other -- X-rays (1895), Becquerel's radioactivity (1896), cathode rays, the luminiferous ether, plus Langmuir's other real cases (mitogenetic rays, the Allison effect, the Davis-Barnes effect). Because those were REAL, the player must actually know which one dissolved.

name: The placebo, and why blinding exists
scope: Sugar pills work -- which is why an honest test must beat one. T1: the strength of a fake treatment scales with how impressive the RITUAL is: two dummy pills beat one, a capsule beats a tablet, and an injection of nothing beats a capsule (the hook: nothing-at-all works better when it looks like more). T2: the design consequence -- the question in a trial is never 'did the patients get better?' but 'did they get better THAN the ones who got the fake?', because most people improve on their own. T3: fake surgery -- in 1959 Leonard Cobb tested a popular chest operation for angina (tying off the internal mammary artery) against a sham in which he cut only the skin; the sham did as well as the real thing, and the operation was abandoned. T4: it happened again in living memory -- Moseley's controlled trial of arthroscopic surgery for knee osteoarthritis, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in July 2002, included a placebo-operated group, and the real surgery did no better. T5: the anti-hype rung -- Hrobjartsson and Gotzsche's 2001 review across some 40 conditions found placebos barely move OBJECTIVE disease outcomes; the clear, repeatable effect is on what the patient reports, above all pain. Placebos mostly change how you feel, not what the disease is doing. T6: even the famous placebo paper fooled itself -- Henry Beecher's 1955 'The Powerful Placebo' fixed the idea that about a third of patients respond, and later reanalysis found much of that was people simply getting better anyway. T7: teach the culprit -- regression to the mean: people join a trial on their WORST day, and worst days are usually followed by better ones no matter what you swallow. T8: the nocebo -- warn people a pill causes headaches and they get headaches; placebo arms of real trials report real side effects, and patients drop out because of them. T9: the strange result -- open-label placebos, where patients are TOLD the pills are inert, still beat no treatment in Ted Kaptchuk's irritable-bowel trials (state the caveat: small studies, subjective outcomes). T10: the brain rung -- in Parkinson's patients, the mere expectation of a drug triggers measurable dopamine release, so 'it's all in your head' names a mechanism rather than dismissing one (verify the imaging study at build before authoring). T11: therefore DOUBLE blind -- not only the patient but the person measuring must be kept in the dark, because the measurer's expectation leaks into the measurement exactly as von Osten's did to Clever Hans.
source: Wikipedia 'Placebo' (Latin 'I shall be pleasing'; Beecher 1955 and the regression-to-the-mean reanalysis; Hrobjartsson & Gotzsche 2001 and the 2010 Cochrane review; open-label placebo findings and their small-sample caveat; nocebo; the pills/capsules/injection dose-of-ritual finding; Parkinson's motor effects); Wikipedia 'Sham surgery' (1959 internal mammary artery ligation as no better than sham; Moseley et al., 'A Controlled Trial of Arthroscopic Surgery for Osteoarthritis of the Knee', NEJM July 2002, treatment group no better than sham). framing_note: Voice: a CONCEPT ladder, so every rung must still be anchored to a named trial or a checkable finding -- never 'what is the placebo effect?'. T1 inverts the wonder: the astonishing fact (an injection of nothing outperforms a pill of nothing) is the HOOK, and the knowable thing is why. Accuracy rail: do NOT overstate the placebo -- the honest modern finding is that placebos reliably move subjective outcomes (pain, nausea) and barely touch objective disease, so T5 is load-bearing and must not be softened into 'the mind heals the body'. Distractor mine: the real rival explanations that fool honest researchers -- spontaneous remission, natural history of the illness, regression to the mean, observer bias, the Hawthorne effect, and (period-correct) animal magnetism. name: The control group: from Lind's six pairs to the randomized trial
scope: The single most powerful idea in medicine is a comparison. T1: 1747 aboard HMS Salisbury -- James Lind takes twelve sailors rotting with scurvy, puts them in the SAME quarters on the SAME basic diet, splits them into six pairs, and gives each pair a different remedy: cider; elixir of vitriol; vinegar; seawater; a paste of garlic, mustard seed and horseradish; and two oranges and a lemon a day. Within about six days the citrus pair are fit for duty (the hook: same air, same food, same hammocks -- only the remedy differed). T2: the invention is not the citrus, it is the DESIGN -- hold everything else identical so the one thing you changed is the only thing that can explain the difference. T3: the honest caveat rung -- Lind did not draw the clean conclusion; he still thought scurvy came from blocked perspiration and putrefaction, and the concentrated citrus 'rob' he later recommended was boiled, which destroyed the very thing that had worked; the Navy did not adopt lemon juice fleet-wide until Gilbert Blane pushed it through in 1795. T4: comparison without counting is not enough either -- in the 1830s Pierre Louis applied his 'numerical method' to bloodletting for pneumonia, simply counting who lived, and found the 2,000-year-old treatment did not help (verify Louis's dates and disease at build). T5: matched groups still fail if the ASSIGNMENT is not fair -- a doctor who chooses who gets the new drug will tend to give it to the patients most likely to do well, and the drug will look good either way. T6: Ronald Fisher's answer was a design, not an argument -- at Rothamsted in the 1920s Muriel Bristol claimed she could taste whether the milk had gone into the cup before or after the tea, and Fisher laid out eight cups, four made each way, presented in random order; there are exactly 70 ways to pick four cups from eight, so getting all four right by luck alone has a 1-in-70 chance. He published the design in The Design of Experiments (1935). T7: what randomizing actually buys -- it balances the differences you thought of AND the ones you never imagined, which is something no amount of careful matching can promise. T8: the first properly randomized clinical trial -- the Medical Research Council's streptomycin trial for tuberculosis, published in 1948 and designed by Austin Bradford Hill, allocated patients by random numbers sealed in envelopes. T9: allocation concealment, the subtle part -- if the doctor can predict which arm the next patient will land in, they can wait for a healthier patient, so the sequence must be hidden even from the enrolling doctor. T10: the ethics rung -- streptomycin was desperately scarce in 1948, and that scarcity is what made randomizing who received it defensible. T11: the modern descendant -- registering in advance which outcome you will measure, so nobody can quietly change the finish line after seeing the data.
source: Wikipedia 'James Lind' and 'Scurvy' (the 1747 HMS Salisbury trial, the six remedies, identical diet and quarters, Lind's own causal beliefs and the boiled rob, Blane and the 1795 Admiralty adoption); Wikipedia 'Randomized controlled trial' (Lind as first reported clinical trial, Fisher's role in randomization, the 1948 MRC streptomycin trial as first published RCT, Bradford Hill); Wikipedia 'Lady tasting tea' (Muriel Bristol, eight cups four each way, 70 combinations, The Design of Experiments 1935); Wikipedia 'Pierre Charles Alexandre Louis' -- VERIFY at build. name: Correlation is not causation
scope: The lurking third thing, taught through a dozen real cases. T1: ice cream sales and drowning deaths climb and fall together, year after year -- the hook; the answer is the hidden third cause that drives both (hot weather sends people to the ice cream counter AND into the water). T2: teach the three ways a correlation can lie before testing them -- a confounder (something causes both), reverse causation (the arrow points the other way), and plain coincidence. T3: the reverse-causation case with a body count -- medieval Europeans concluded lice kept a person healthy, because sick people had almost none; in fact lice abandon a feverish body, so the illness drove the lice away rather than the lice keeping illness off. T4: a research reversal a kid can follow -- a 1999 study reported that children who slept with a night light were far likelier to become nearsighted; a follow-up found the real link was that nearsighted PARENTS, who pass on nearsightedness, were the ones who left the light on (verify both studies at build). T5: the biggest reversal of them all -- observational studies showed that women taking hormone therapy after menopause had fewer heart attacks, and it became standard advice; the randomized Women's Health Initiative trial was stopped in July 2002 when the combined estrogen-plus-progestin arm showed INCREASED coronary disease and stroke. The confounder was healthy-user bias: the women who took it were already healthier, wealthier and better screened. T6: how you break the tie -- randomizing severs the link between who gets the treatment and everything else about them, which is why the trial could overturn decades of observation. T7: even the inventor of randomization fooled himself -- Ronald Fisher argued in the 1950s that smoking might not cause lung cancer, proposing an unmeasured genetic factor that caused both the smoking and the cancer; he was a heavy pipe smoker and a paid consultant to tobacco firms, and he was wrong. T8: how that case was actually won WITHOUT randomizing people -- Doll and Hill followed British doctors for decades and found dose-response (more cigarettes, more cancer), risk falling after quitting, and a mechanism in tissue; Bradford Hill's 1965 list set out when a correlation has earned the word 'cause' (verify Doll/Hill details at build). T9: correlations by sheer volume -- Tyler Vigen's spurious-correlation collection pairs things like cheese consumption and bizarre accident deaths at near-perfect correlation; search enough pairs and stunning matches appear from chance alone. T10: the Texas sharpshooter -- fire at a barn wall, then paint the target around the tightest cluster; picking the pattern after seeing the data is the same move. T11: the three questions a kid can ask at dinner -- could Y be causing X? what third thing could cause both? has anyone ever randomized it?
source: Wikipedia 'Correlation does not imply causation' (ice cream and drownings and the summer confounder; the night-light/myopia study and the parental-myopia follow-up; HDL cholesterol; the medieval lice reversal; confounder / reverse causation / coincidence vocabulary); Wikipedia 'Women's Health Initiative' (observational cardioprotection claim, trial halted July 2002 after 5.2 years, increased coronary heart disease/stroke/pulmonary embolism, healthy-user bias); Wikipedia 'Ronald Fisher' (his constitutional/genetic-confounder argument in the early 1950s, tobacco-firm consultancy, pipe smoking); Wikipedia 'Spurious correlation' / Tyler Vigen. Accuracy rail: the WHI rung must state the specific arm and outcome (combined estrogen-plus-progestin, stopped July 2002, more heart disease and stroke) and must not be flattened into 'hormones are bad'. name: Wason's 2-4-6 and the urge to confirm
scope: Confirmation bias as a game you can lose in ninety seconds. T1: the setup -- you are told 2, 4, 6 fits a hidden rule, and you may test any triple you like and be told only yes or no. Almost everyone offers 8-10-12, then 20-22-24, then 100-102-104, gets 'yes' every time, and announces with confidence: add two each time. The rule was simply ANY three numbers in increasing order (the hook: every test came back yes and the answer was still wrong). T2: the winning move -- propose a triple you EXPECT to be told no, like 1-2-3 or 6-4-2, because only a 'no' shows you where your rule's edge really is; a string of yeses from tests that could never fail teaches nothing. T3: the source -- Peter Wason's 1960 paper 'On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task', which is where the term confirmation bias comes from. T4: Wason's other trap, the four-card selection task (1966; published 1968) -- four cards show 3, 8, blue and red, each with a number on one face and a colour on the other, and the rule is 'if a card shows an even number on one face, its opposite face is blue'. Fewer than one person in ten picks correctly: you must turn the 8 AND the red card. T5: why the blue card is the tempting mistake -- turning it can only ever confirm; whatever is on its back, the rule survives. The red card is the only other card that can BREAK the rule. T6: the same puzzle becomes easy when it is about catching a cheat -- 'if you are drinking beer you must be over eighteen', with cards reading beer, cola, 25 and 16, and most people instantly check the beer drinker and the sixteen-year-old (Griggs and Cox, 1982 -- verify at build). T7: what science does with this -- the strong test is the one that could have come out against you, which is why a prediction that fits every possible result is worthless however impressive it sounds. T8: the home version -- before you argue for your idea, write down in advance what observation would make you drop it; if you cannot name one, you are playing 2-4-6 with yourself.

framing_note: Voice: the most PLAYABLE ladder in the strand -- T1 must run the game in the stem (the three triples that all came back yes) and make the hidden rule the answer, so the player experiences the trap rather than being told about it. Accuracy rail: the 2-4-6 rule is 'any ascending sequence' -- not 'any three numbers', not 'even numbers' -- and Wason's selection-task success figure is under 10%, replicated in 1993; keep both exact. Second rail: the abstract card task and the drinking-age version are the SAME logical problem, and that equivalence is the point of T6, so state it plainly. Dinner-test payoff: T1 -- it is the rung a father can run on his kids at the table. Distractor mine: the plausible wrong rules real subjects announce ('increases by two', 'the middle number is the average of the other two', 'even numbers ascending') and, for the card task, the tempting blue card. Lane border: PHILOSOPHY owns Popper and falsificationism as an epistemology topic -- this ladder keys Wason's ACTUAL EXPERIMENT and its measured results, never 'what did Popper argue?'.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank: Popper, falsificationism, and the logic of hypothesis testing as seminar moves. Guard by anchoring every rung to Wason's experiments, the specific card layouts and the measured success rates.

name: Sagan's dragon in the garage
scope: A claim that dodges every possible test has quietly stopped claiming anything. T1: 'A fire-breathing dragon lives in my garage.' You reach for a camera -- she's invisible. You spread flour to catch footprints -- she floats. You bring an infrared sensor for the fire -- the fire is heatless. You try to spray-paint her outline -- she's incorporeal. Sagan's question is the answer rung: 'what's the difference between an invisible, incorporeal, floating dragon who spits heatless fire and no dragon at all?' T2: the structural point -- every excuse arrived only AFTER a test was proposed; a claim rebuilt on the spot to survive each new test has stopped predicting anything, and a claim that predicts nothing cannot be checked by anyone, including you. T3: where it comes from -- The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark (1995), Sagan's last book, written for exactly this purpose. T4: the baloney detection kit, the part a kid can use tonight -- seek independent confirmation; encourage debate from people who disagree; arguments from authority carry little weight; think up more than one hypothesis; do not get attached to a hypothesis because it is YOURS; quantify where you can; every link in the chain must hold; and prefer the simpler explanation. T5: the ninth rule is the strand's spine -- the claim must be falsifiable; if no imaginable observation could count against it, it is not a claim about the world. T6: the honest counterweight rung -- Sagan insisted this was not licence to sneer: science needs an almost impossible balance of openness to new ideas AND ruthless scrutiny of them, and dropping either half wrecks it. T7: the pedigree of the slogan -- 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence' is Sagan's phrasing of an older idea, close to Marcello Truzzi's 1970s wording and to Laplace's much earlier version; credit the lineage rather than treating it as Sagan's invention.
source: Wikipedia 'The Demon-Haunted World' (the dragon parable and its escalating excuses, the concluding question quoted verbatim, the nine-item baloney detection kit, the catalogue of fallacies, 1995 publication); Wikipedia 'Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence' (Sagan, Truzzi, Laplace lineage) -- VERIFY the lineage wording at build. Accuracy rail: the Sagan question must be quoted exactly as written ('an invisible, incorporeal, floating dragon who spits heatless fire') or not quoted at all; do not attach any unsourced Sagan aphorism to this ladder, and do not quote T6 -- paraphrase the openness-plus-scrutiny balance rather than inventing a line. Second rail: 'extraordinary claims' predates Sagan -- the credit rung is the interesting one, so do not let a rung imply he coined it. Dinner-test payoff: T1. Distractor mine: real adjacent principles a bright kid might confuse -- Occam's razor, the burden of proof, argument from ignorance, ad hominem, and Hitchens's razor -- all real, so the player must know which one the dragon illustrates. Lane border: PHILOSOPHY owns Popper's demarcation criterion and the fallacy catalogue as seminar content; this ladder is the PARABLE and the practical checklist only. If a contrast rung is wanted (a claim that DID risk being wrong), name Einstein's 1919 eclipse prediction in a single clause and leave the physics to that sub-strand.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank: falsifiability/demarcation (Popper), Occam's razor, and named informal fallacies. Guard by keying every rung to Sagan's own text and the kit's practical rules rather than to any philosopher's argument.

name: Feynman, the O-ring and the glass of ice water
scope: One simple test cuts through a bureaucracy's fog. T1: 11 February 1986, a live televised hearing of the Rogers Commission -- Feynman takes a scrap of the shuttle booster's O-ring rubber, squeezes it flat in a C-clamp, drops it in his glass of ice water, fishes it out and shows that it does not spring back (the hook: the whole investigation turned on a glass of ice water on the witness table). T2: what an O-ring does -- a rubber ring sealing the joints between segments of the solid rocket booster, whose entire job is to squeeze back instantly and block hot gas the moment the joint flexes at ignition. T3: the temperature -- the morning of 28 January 1986 the pad sat at roughly 28-29 F, far below the coldest previous launch at 53 F. T4: the night before, Morton Thiokol engineers including Roger Boisjoly argued against launching in that cold; the company's no-launch recommendation was reversed before morning. T5: who pointed Feynman at it -- Air Force General Donald Kutyna steered him toward the cold, wrapping the hint in a casual question about a car's seals; a 2013 BBC documentary revealed that Sally Ride had quietly passed Kutyna NASA test data showing the rings stiffened when chilled. T6: the deeper finding, and the one Feynman cared about -- he asked NASA managers and working engineers separately for the odds of catastrophic failure: management said about 1 in 100,000 launches, engineers said 1 in 50 to 1 in 200, and Feynman put it near 1 in 100. T7: Appendix F -- Feynman insisted his dissenting appendix be included in the report, and it ends: 'For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled.' T8: the institutional failure named -- O-ring erosion had appeared on earlier flights and been treated as evidence the design TOLERATED damage rather than as a warning; the sociologist Diane Vaughan later called this the normalization of deviance (verify her term and book at build). T9: MYTH CORRECTION -- the shuttle did not detonate like a bomb; hot gas escaping the failed joint broke the external tank apart, its hydrogen and oxygen burned in the open, and the orbiter was torn apart by aerodynamic forces. Tell it soberly and factually. T10: what a kid takes away -- the commission had thousands of pages of analysis; the thing that settled it was a piece of rubber, a clamp and cold water, a test anyone in the room could see and anyone at home could repeat.
source: Wikipedia 'Rogers Commission Report' (the televised ice-water/clamp demonstration and Feynman's description of the rubber not springing back; Kutyna's tip and the 2013 BBC documentary on Sally Ride's data; management's 1-in-100,000 versus engineers' 1-in-50-to-1-in-200 and Feynman's own 1-in-100; the exact final line of Appendix F); Wikipedia 'Space Shuttle Challenger disaster' (28-29 F launch morning versus 53 F previous minimum; Boisjoly and the Thiokol teleconference; the vehicle breakup mechanism); Diane Vaughan, 'The Challenger Launch Decision' -- VERIFY the term at build. Grokipedia 403 to the harness this session; re-check at build.
framing_note: Voice: T1 keys the ACT and the object (rubber, C-clamp, ice water, live TV) and the answer is what it proved about the seal at freezing -- never a date question and never 'who investigated Challenger?'. This ladder starts at T2 because the subject matter needs a little scaffolding; there is no T1 rung. Accuracy rail: Appendix F's final line must be quoted exactly ('...for nature cannot be fooled') and attributed to the appendix, not to the commission's main report; and the Kutyna car story is Kutyna's own later telling, so say 'by Kutyna's account'. Second rail: handle the loss of the crew soberly and briefly -- no dwelling, no gore; the myth-correction rung exists because 'it exploded' is the near-universal misconception, and the correction is told plainly. Dinner-test payoff: T1. Distractor mine: the real failure hypotheses investigators had to eliminate -- main engine failure, external tank rupture as the initiating event, structural failure of a strut, debris strike, sabotage -- plus real adjacent shuttle facts. STANCE: this is one of the two rungs in this sub-strand where the bank's own voice is genuinely engaged -- an institution's public-relations number beat its engineers' number, and the bank PRESENTS that in Feynman's own words without editorializing about NASA.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank: the Challenger disaster as a 1980s American national event, Christa McAuliffe and Teacher in Space, the Reagan address. Guard by keying every rung to the PHYSICS (rubber resilience at low temperature, the joint seal, the breakup mechanism) and the probability finding; leave the national-mourning story to history.

name: Survivorship bias: Wald's bombers and the missing data
scope: You are always looking at the survivors. T1: 1943, the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University -- the military brings Abraham Wald diagrams of bullet holes in bombers that made it home, clustered on the wings and fuselage, and asks where to add armour; Wald's answer is to armour the places with NO holes (the hook: reinforce where the returning planes were undamaged). T2: the reasoning -- planes hit in the engines and cockpit are not in the sample, because they did not come back; the holes you can see mark the damage a bomber can SURVIVE. T3: the honest caveat rung -- the vivid scene of Wald pointing at a diagram is a retelling; his real contribution was a set of technical memoranda giving a method to estimate how vulnerable each part was, inferred from the damage on the planes that returned. T4: the same bias in the scientific literature -- studies that find nothing are harder to publish, so they stay in the drawer and the published record looks stronger than reality; Robert Rosenthal named it the file-drawer problem in 1979 (verify at build). T5: the psychic version -- Martin Gardner's point about J. B. Rhine's card-guessing experiments is that if you test enough people, a few will produce astonishing streaks by chance alone; report only those and you have discovered nothing at all. T6: everyday versions worth a rung each -- 'college dropouts get rich' (you never meet the dropouts who did not), 'old buildings were built better' (the badly built ones fell down), 'people who take this supplement are healthier' (healthier people are the ones who take supplements). T7: the fix -- decide in advance who counts, count everyone you started with, and publish the failures; this is the same discipline that preregistration enforces on a modern trial.
source: Wikipedia 'Survivorship bias' (Wald at the Statistical Research Group, Columbia, 1943; the armour-where-there-are-no-holes inference; the memoranda and the caveat that the popular retelling oversimplifies; Martin Gardner on J. B. Rhine's card-guessing subjects; the Academy Award longevity reanalysis as an immortal-time-bias example); Rosenthal 1979 file-drawer problem -- VERIFY at build. This ladder has no T1-easy rung; it starts at T2. Accuracy rail: the caveat rung is mandatory -- Wald's actual work was eight statistical memoranda, and the dramatized 'Wald points at the map' scene should be told as the popular retelling of a real result, not as documented dialogue; never put invented quotes in Wald's mouth. Dinner-test payoff: T1. Distractor mine: the neighbouring biases, all real and all confusable -- selection bias, regression to the mean, confirmation bias, publication bias, the Texas sharpshooter -- so the player must know which one the bombers illustrate. Lane border: HISTORY owns the WWII bombing campaigns; every answer here is a statistical move, not a war fact.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank: the WWII strategic bombing campaign and American wartime scientific mobilization. Guard by keying every rung to the inference (the unseen sample) rather than to the air war. Within-bank: the file-drawer rung overlaps the replication-crisis ladder -- keep the NAMED file-drawer coinage here and let the replication ladder own preregistration and the measured replication rates.

name: Emily Rosa, aged eleven, in a medical journal
scope: A fourth-grader's science fair project that tested a claim no adult had bothered to test. T1: the setup -- nine-year-old Emily Rosa sat practitioners at a table with a cardboard screen between them, had them push their hands through two holes, flipped a coin to choose left or right, held her own hand above one of theirs, and asked which hand could feel her energy field (the hook: the entire apparatus was a screen and a coin). T2: what was being tested -- Therapeutic Touch, whose practitioners said they could sense and smooth a human energy field with their hands without touching the patient, and which was being taught in nursing schools at the time. T3: the result -- 21 practitioners, ten tries each, averaged 4.4 correct out of 10, where blind guessing would give 5; the paper appeared in the Journal of the American Medical Association on 1 April 1998, making Rosa the youngest person ever to publish in a major medical journal. T4: why the screen IS the experiment -- it strips away every cue except the one being claimed, which is the same move as the blindfold in Franklin's garden and the blinders on Clever Hans; JAMA's editor George Lundberg put the principle plainly: 'Age doesn't matter. It's good science that matters, and this is good science.' T5: the honest caveats rung -- the study was small and single-blind, some practitioners objected that the conditions were not right, and Therapeutic Touch is still practised; the bank states this without a verdict and lets the test speak.
source: Wikipedia 'Emily Rosa' (age nine at the 1996 fourth-grade science fair, publication April 1998 as the youngest person published in a peer-reviewed medical journal, the screen-and-hands protocol, 21 practitioners across two series, an average 4.4 of 10 correct, JAMA 1 April 1998, George Lundberg's quoted remark, the Scientific American Frontiers filming of the second series). name: The replication crisis and the fix
scope: Science catching itself fooling itself, in public, with numbers. T1: in 2015 Brian Nosek's Open Science Collaboration had roughly 270 researchers redo 100 published psychology experiments by the book -- only about 36% came out statistically significant again, and the effects that survived were on average half the original size (the hook: a third, not a rounding error). T2: it is not only psychology -- Amgen scientists reported that only 6 of 53 landmark preclinical cancer studies could be confirmed (about 11%), and Bayer researchers put their own in-house replication of published findings at around a quarter. T3: how this happens with nobody lying -- Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn's 2011 paper 'False-Positive Psychology' showed that ordinary analytic flexibility (drop the outliers or not, add ten more subjects or stop, report which of four measures worked) can push the false-positive rate above 60%, and they used it to 'demonstrate' something impossible about a Beatles song and listeners' ages. T4: the name for the move -- p-hacking, or the garden of forking paths: run many analyses, report the one that came out, and the published result looks like a single clean test that it never was. T5: the shock that broke the dam -- in 2011 Daryl Bem published experiments in a top journal apparently showing people could sense future events; the alarming part was that his methods were STANDARD practice, so if standard practice can deliver precognition, standard practice is the problem. T6: John Ioannidis argued the arithmetic in 2005 in a paper titled 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' -- in fields that test many hypotheses with small studies, most published positive findings will be wrong even when everyone is honest. T7: the fix that works -- preregistration and registered reports: you publish your prediction and your analysis plan BEFORE you collect data, and the journal accepts the paper on the strength of the design rather than the result, which removes the incentive to hunt for a finding. T8: the counterweight rung, and the strand's closing note -- this crisis was discovered BY scientists, running replications on purpose, and published where anyone can read it; that is the same self-correction that killed N-rays and polywater. A consensus is not evidence; a replicated result is.
source: Wikipedia 'Replication crisis' (Open Science Collaboration 2015, 100 studies, ~36% replication and halved effect sizes, the per-journal and per-subfield breakdowns; Begley & Ellis 2012 Amgen 6 of 53 / 11%; the Bayer quarter figure; Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn 2011 'False-Positive Psychology' and the >60% false-positive demonstration; Daryl Bem's 2011 precognition papers and why the community found the standard methods upsetting; Ioannidis 2005 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'; preregistration and Brian Nosek / Center for Open Science). framing_note: Voice: the modern spine of 'you are the easiest person to fool' -- T1 inverts the wonder by putting the measured number in the stem and making the WHAT (a deliberate mass replication of 100 published studies) the answer. Accuracy rail: quote the figures precisely and in their proper frame -- about 36% replicated with significance, effect sizes about half; 6 of 53 for Amgen; and NEVER slide into 'most science is fake'. Failure to replicate is not proof the original was false, and the T8 counterweight rung is mandatory so the ladder lands on self-correction rather than cynicism. Second rail: verify the specific 'False-Positive Psychology' demonstration before authoring it as a rung; if it does not check out, key T3 to the >60% false-positive result alone. Third rail: Bem's work is presented as a methodological lesson, never as evidence for or against psychic phenomena. Dinner-test payoff: T1. Distractor mine: real neighbouring failure modes -- publication bias, the file-drawer problem, HARKing, small-sample noise, outright fraud -- so the player must know which one each case names. STANCE: this is the sub-strand's second genuinely stance-engaged ladder; the bank honours the replicating dissenters and names the institutional incentives plainly, in numbers, and stops there.
